messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is a 34-year-old parole officer who came to therapy at his partner’s urging after a colleague noticed he had started flinching whenever a male parolee entered his office. The trouble had been building for two years, ever since the night his former boyfriend, Marcus, beat him so badly that Kofi ended up in the emergency room with a fractured orbital bone and three cracked ribs. He had gone to the hospital alone, too ashamed to call anyone, and the antiseptic smell of the ER—bleach and iodine and hand sanitizer—had stayed lodged in his sinuses. Eighteen months later, that same smell could still ambush him: a whiff of disinfectant in a public restroom, the sting of hand sanitizer on a coworker’s desk, and suddenly he was back in that trauma bay, the fluorescent lights too bright, the crunch of his own ribs audible beneath the nurse’s gloved hands. He would taste the metallic tang of blood in his mouth, the same taste he had had that night, and for a few seconds the memory did not feel like a memory at all—it felt as though the attack was happening right now, in the present, and he would have to grip the edge of his desk to remind himself where he was.

At work, Kofi’s body stayed on permanent alert. His shoulders were drawn up, his jaw tight, his eyes constantly moving—scanning the waiting room, watching the hands of every man who walked into his cubicle. He avoided eye contact because he had learned, the hard way, that looking directly at someone felt like an invitation. When Marcus had looked at him that way—a certain slant of appraisal, a sexualized scrutiny—violence had followed. Now Kofi did not want anyone to look at him like that again, so he kept his gaze down, his face neutral, his body small. He also avoided any situation that smelled like confrontation. If a parolee arrived angry or demanding, Kofi would agree to whatever the man wanted just to end the interaction, even if it meant bending the rules. He had stopped calling violations. He had stopped pushing back. His supervisor had started to notice that his caseload was oddly quiet, and that some of his clients were showing up with infractions that should have been documented but were not. Kofi told himself it was not worth the risk—disagreements led to raised voices, and raised voices led to the floor coming up at him.

At home, Kofi had come to believe that his life was fundamentally broken. He would say to his partner, “What happened to me was unfair, and nothing was ever done about it.” Marcus had never been charged; Kofi had never filed a report. The injustice sat inside him like a stone. He had begun to push away positive emotions—when his partner reached for him in bed, when a friend made him laugh, when he felt a flicker of happiness—because those moments felt dangerous. They were the kind of moment that preceded the attack: a good evening, a shared joke, and then the switch. So he learned to stay flat. He learned not to feel too much. Some nights he lay awake and thought that maybe his life was not worth living anymore, though he never said it aloud and never made a plan. It was just a thought that drifted in and stayed.

Two weeks before his first session, a new male parolee was assigned to Kofi. The man was tall, broad-shouldered, and when he sat down across from Kofi he leaned forward and held eye contact a beat too long. The smell of cheap deodorant and stale sweat hit Kofi’s nose. He heard Marcus’s voice in his head—a specific growl that meant the beating was coming—and Kofi’s hands began to shake. He excused himself, walked to the bathroom, and stood with his forehead against the cold tile until the taste of blood left his mouth. He called his partner that evening and said, finally, “I think I need help.” He was terrified that if he let himself feel any hope about therapy, hope itself would become another thing to be punished for. But he was more terrified of the moment when the memory stopped feeling like a flashback and started making him believe that the attack was still happening, that it would never be over.
